studies.citation: Ali, J. R. and Cunich, P. (2001) 'The orientation of churches: some new evidence', The Antiquaries Journal 81: 155-193. doi:10.1017/S0003581500072188
studies.finding: A magnetic compass was not used; sunrise or sunset on the patron's feast day could explain up to 43% of the churches, and Easter Day or equinox sunrise most of the rest.
studies.sample: 143 sites, mostly mid-11th to late 12th century cathedrals, large churches and monastic ruins, England

sources.title: The Orientation of Churches: Some New Evidence
sources.author: Ali and Cunich (Cambridge Core abstract)
sources.quote: Wordsworth's basic hypothesis might hold for as many as 43 per cent of the churches if sunrise and sunset positions are considered

studies.citation: Hinton, I. (2006) 'Church alignment and patronal saint's days', The Antiquaries Journal 86: 206-226. doi:10.1017/S0003581500000111
studies.finding: Churches of saints with summer and winter feasts face the same way, so they were not laid out to their patron's sunrise; mean alignment differs by 10 degrees between west and east England.

sources.title: Church Alignment and Patronal Saint's Days
sources.author: Hinton (Cambridge Core abstract)
sources.quote: The results of this survey of almost 1,500 rural churches do not support the oft-repeated idea that churches are aligned with their patronal saint's sunrise.

sources.title: Church Alignment and Patronal Saint's Days
sources.author: Hinton (Cambridge Core abstract)
sources.quote: churches dedicated to saints with summer feast-days are aligned in the same direction as those dedicated to saints with winter feast-days

studies.citation: Hoare, P. G. (2015) 'Orientation of English medieval parish churches', in C. L. N. Ruggles (ed.) Handbook of Archaeoastronomy and Ethnoastronomy, New York: Springer, 1711-1718. doi:10.1007/978-1-4614-6141-8_174
studies.finding: A review of three centuries of work: few church alignments are explained beyond doubt and most tests of the feast-day theory are not rigorous enough to settle it.

sources.title: Orientation of English Medieval Parish Churches
sources.author: Hoare (Springer abstract)
sources.quote: tests of the overwhelmingly popular festival orientation theory are often insufficiently rigorous to provide convincing answers

studies.finding: Summary: some churches (e.g. St Stephen's, Vienna) face sunrise on their patron's day, but a 2006 survey of old English churches found practically no relationship with the feast days.

sources.title: Orientation of churches
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: However, a survey of old English churches published in 2006 showed practically no relationship with the feast days of the saints to whom they are dedicated.

sources.title: Orientation of churches
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: some churches seem to be oriented to sunrise on the feast day of their patron saint.

studies.citation: González-García, A. C. and Belmonte, J. A. (2015) 'The orientation of pre-Romanesque churches in the Iberian Peninsula', Nexus Network Journal 17: 353-377. doi:10.1007/s00004-014-0231-7
studies.finding: Comparison outside the isles: early churches cluster on the canonical equinox (25 March) and sunrise on the patron's day is completely absent.
studies.sample: 167 churches built before AD 1086, Iberian Peninsula (not the British Isles)

sources.title: The Orientation of Pre-Romanesque Churches in the Iberian Peninsula
sources.author: González-García and Belmonte (Springer abstract)
sources.quote: popular 'expected' orientations, such as that of the rising sun on the day of the patron saint of the church, are completely absent.
